stores.summary: Each row in this table captures a single retail outlet – a physical store or shop – and records its identifying details, such as a unique numeric store ID, the store’s name (often the city plus a location label like “Main” or “Plaza”), the city where it operates, the two‑letter state abbreviation, and the calendar date it opened in the standard YYYY‑MM‑DD format. The data are used to answer everyday business questions about locations, such as how many stores exist in a particular city or state, which locations opened in a given year, trends in new openings over time, or comparisons of store counts across regions. Users might ask about “store count,” “outlet locations,” “branch openings,” “new shops,” or “regional coverage.” The store_id serves as the primary key, store_name is a descriptive label, city is the full city name, state follows the official two‑letter US codes, and opened_date records the exact opening day; any missing dates should be treated as unknown and omitted from time‑based totals, while null values in city or state indicate incomplete location data and should not be included in geographic aggregations.

employees.summary: Each row in this table captures a single staff member – an individual person who works for the company – and records the basic personal and employment details that define that employee’s role in the business. The data are used to answer everyday workforce questions such as how many people are on the payroll, how many sales associates or cashiers are assigned to each store, what the total or average compensation is by title, store or hire year, and how many employees report to a particular manager. Users might ask about headcount, staff levels, wages, salary budget, tenure, or manager‑employee relationships, using words like “employees,” “personnel,” “workers,” “pay,” “salary,” “compensation,” “job title,” “role,” “store,” “manager,” or “supervisor.” The key fields are employee_id, a unique numeric identifier; first_name and last_name for the person’s name; title, which is limited to Store Manager, Sales Associate, Senior Sales Associate, Cashier, or Inventory Specialist; store_id indicating the store location; manager_id pointing to the employee’s direct manager (null only for Store Managers, who have no higher manager); hire_date stored as a text string in YYYY‑MM‑DD format that shows when the person started; and salary, an integer representing annual pay in US dollars. When calculating totals or averages, salary should be treated as a whole‑dollar amount, hire_date should be parsed as a calendar date, and rows with a null manager_id are not counted as reporting staff but still count toward overall headcount and salary sums.

customers.summary: Each record captures a single individual who has created an account, representing a customer, client, user or subscriber in the real world. The table lets analysts answer questions such as how many customers exist, how many signed up each month or year, which cities or states have the most accounts, and how to look up a person by name or email address. People will ask about “customers,” “users,” “accounts,” “sign‑ups,” “registrations,” or “client count.” The key fields are a unique numeric customer_id that identifies the person, first_name and last_name for personal identification, and email which holds the contact address. The city column stores the city name exactly as entered, so variations like “New York,” “NY,” “NYC,” or lower‑case “new york” all refer to the same place and may need normalisation; the state column holds a two‑letter US state code. The signup_date is stored as text in ISO format YYYY‑MM‑DD and can be used for trend analysis over time. When aggregating by location, rows with a blank or null city or state should be excluded from city/state counts, and any future dates (e.g., 2025‑07‑28) should be treated according to the reporting period rather than automatically discarded.

suppliers.summary: Each record in this table describes a single supplier – a company that provides goods or services to the business – and includes the supplier’s unique identifier, its official name, the country where it operates, and the email address of the sales contact. The table is useful whenever users need to look up who supplies what, count how many suppliers come from a particular region, compare the distribution of suppliers across countries, or retrieve the appropriate contact email for outreach or contract management. People might ask about “vendors,” “suppliers,” “partners,” “source companies,” or “providers” and may use terms like “where are our suppliers located,” “how many vendors do we have in Asia,” or “what is the email for the sales rep at a given supplier.” The key fields are supplier_id, an internal numeric key; supplier_name, the business name; country, a short text code such as USA, China, or Germany indicating the supplier’s base; and contact_email, the sales contact address, which may be blank if no email is on file. The identifier is guaranteed to be unique, country values follow standard country names, and any missing email should be treated as unavailable rather than zero when aggregating contact information.

products.summary: Each record in this table describes a single product that a company offers for sale, capturing the item’s unique identifier, its descriptive name, the market segment it belongs to, the vendor that supplies it, and the current list price. Users can query this data to find how many products exist in each category such as electronics, home & kitchen, clothing, sports & outdoors, or books, to compare average or total list prices across categories or suppliers, to look up the price of a specific item by name or SKU, and to rank suppliers by the number of products they provide. Common language people use includes “product,” “item,” “merchandise,” “SKU,” “price,” “cost,” “list price,” “catalog,” “category,” and “supplier.” The key fields are the product ID (a unique numeric key), product name (the textual label), category (a predefined set of segment names), supplier ID (the numeric code of the vendor, which may be blank if unknown and should be ignored in supplier‑based aggregates), and unit_price_cents (the price in cents, which must be divided by 100 to express dollars). Prices are always list prices, not discounted amounts, and a null price should be treated as missing and excluded from any monetary totals.

orders.summary: Each row in this table records a single purchase transaction made by a shopper, capturing the moment a customer placed an order at a particular store and which staff member processed it. The data is used to answer questions about total sales volume, order counts, daily or monthly trends, store‑by‑store performance, employee productivity, and the proportion of orders that are still processing, shipped, delivered or cancelled. Users might ask about “orders,” “purchases,” “sales,” “transactions,” “store revenue,” “employee sales,” or “order status.” The key fields are the order identifier, the customer identifier linking to the buyer, the store identifier indicating where the sale occurred, the employee identifier for the associate handling the sale, the order date stored as a text string in MM/DD/YYYY format that must be converted to a proper date for any time‑based analysis, and the status text that can be “delivered” (order received by the customer), “shipped” (in transit), “processing” (not yet shipped), or “cancelled” (order voided and should be omitted from revenue calculations). A cancelled status means the record has no line‑item details and must be excluded when summing sales or counting fulfilled orders.

order_items.summary: Each row records a single product line on a customer purchase, capturing exactly how many units of a specific item were bought and the price paid for each unit at the moment the order was placed. The table lets analysts total up sales dollars, count how many items were sold, see which products generate the most revenue, track average price per unit, compare purchase volumes across time periods, and look up the details of any individual order line. People will ask about “sales”, “revenue”, “units sold”, “quantity”, “price”, “spend”, “order lines” or “product purchases”. The key fields are the line‑item identifier, the order identifier that groups multiple lines together, the product identifier that tells which SKU was bought, the quantity column that holds the number of units (normally a positive integer), and the unit_price_cents column that stores the price per unit in cents, so the dollar amount for the line is quantity × unit_price_cents ÷ 100. When calculating totals, multiply quantity by unit_price_cents and divide by 100 to get dollars; rows with a null or zero quantity should be ignored because they do not represent a real purchase.

payments.summary: Each record in this table captures a single payment that a customer made for an order, showing how much money was taken, the way it was paid, and whether the charge was kept or returned. The data is used to answer questions such as total revenue, average spend per order, how many transactions were completed versus refunded, which payment methods are most popular, and trends in refunds over time. Users might ask about sales, revenue, purchases, spend, refunds, payment types, credit‑card versus PayPal usage, or how much money was returned to customers. The key fields are the payment identifier, the order reference, the payment method (credit_card, debit_card, paypal, or gift_card), the amount charged stored in cents (so 7996 represents $79.96), and the status flag where “completed” means the money stayed with the business and “refunded” means the amount was returned to the buyer. When calculating totals, only rows with status = completed should be included; refunded rows represent cancellations and should be excluded from net sales, while they can be summed separately to measure refund volume. Null values do not appear in the sample, and any missing method or status would be treated as unknown and omitted from method‑specific breakdowns.

shipments.summary: Each row records a single physical shipment that moves an order from the store to the customer, capturing the logistics event for that order. The table lets analysts answer questions such as how many packages were sent, which carrier—UPS, FedEx, USPS, or DHL—handles the most volume, average time between the ship date and the delivery date, trends in on‑time deliveries over months, counts of pending or cancelled shipments, and comparisons of carrier performance for a given period. Users will ask about “shipments,” “deliveries,” “dispatches,” “fulfillment,” “logistics,” “transport,” or “shipping” when they need to see totals, percentages, or trends. The key fields are a unique shipment identifier, the associated order number, the carrier name, the ship date (a YYYY‑MM‑DD string that is NULL until the package leaves the store), the delivery date (same format, NULL until the package reaches the customer), and a status flag that can be “delivered,” “in_transit,” “pending” (not yet shipped) or “cancelled.” A NULL ship or delivery date means the event has not occurred, and cancelled rows should be excluded from on‑time or transit calculations, while pending rows count toward outstanding shipments.

reviews.summary: Each row in this table captures a single customer’s feedback about a specific product, recording the moment the comment was posted and the star rating the shopper assigned. The data is used to answer questions such as how many reviews a product has received, the average rating across a time period, trends in customer satisfaction over months, which items are most praised or most criticized, and to look up the exact text of a comment for quality‑control or marketing purposes. People will refer to this information with words like “reviews,” “ratings,” “customer feedback,” “star score,” “comments,” “sentiment,” or “product opinions.” The key fields are the unique review identifier, the product identifier that tells which item is being evaluated, the customer identifier linking the comment to a shopper, the numeric rating that ranges from one (poor) to five (excellent), the free‑form review text, and the review date stored in a YYYY‑MM‑DD format. A rating of zero never appears, and a missing review_text simply means the customer left a star rating without a written comment; dates outside the expected range should be excluded from time‑based analyses.
